title: De insigni paradoxo, quod in analysi maximorum et minimorum occurrit

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. The functional is the 'momentum' M = ∫ √x ds, i.e. the Maupertuis action ∫ v ds for a heavy body. Here x is the depth below the horizontal line fh on which the speed vanishes. F lies at depth f, H at depth h, and their horizontal separation is 2g. The extremals are parabolas, which are projectile trajectories with the fixed energy.

Results from the previous page. Euler found two extremal arcs, distinguished by the sign of √(fh−gg). He gave the action of one of them as M = (2/3)(f+h−√(fh−gg))·√(f+h+2√(fh−gg)).

§13 to the top of p.24 (existence). The arcs are real only if gg ≤ fh. In modern terms H must lie inside the 'safety parabola' whose focus is F and whose directrix is the line x = −f. Distance to F ≤ distance to the directrix gives 4g² + (h−f)² ≤ (h+f)², i.e. g² ≤ fh. If gg > fh the curve becomes imaginary.

§14 (boundary case). When gg = fh the two arcs coalesce and H lies on the envelope (the 'longest throw'). Then M_arc = (2/3)(f+h)^{3/2}. Euler compares this with the broken path F→f→h→H: straight up to the zero-speed line, along it, and straight down. Its action is ∫₀^f √x dx + 0 + ∫₀^h √x dx = (2/3)(f^{3/2} + h^{3/2}). This is always smaller, because t^{3/2} is superadditive. So the 'minimum' supplied by the calculus is beaten by another admissible path. That is the paradox of the title.

§15 (explanation). The broken path is itself a minimum 'in its kind': perturbing f and h increases the action. The calculus did not show it because it is not a continuous (smooth) line. Yet it does satisfy the first integral p√x/√(1+pp) = C with C = 0 on every piece:
- on the vertical pieces because p = 0;
- on the horizontal piece because x = 0.

On the next page Euler adds that a function can have several local minima, so both parabolic arcs can be 'minima' even when their values differ greatly.

In modern language this is a Goldschmidt-type discontinuous (broken) extremal, compared with smooth extremals. It runs along the degenerate boundary of the Jacobi–Maupertuis metric, where path length costs nothing. The boundary case is the conjugate-point/envelope (caustic) situation of Jacobi's theory.
errors: The formula carried over to this page, (2/3)(f+h−√)·√(f+h+2√), with √ = √(fh−gg), is the high-lob branch. For f = h and g → 0 it gives (4/3)f^{3/2}, the same as going straight up and back down. The low branch is (2/3)(f+h+√)·√(f+h−2√), which tends to 0. Euler does not say clearly which branch is which.

In §14 Euler says the coalesced arc (gg = fh) is 'in suo genere minimum'. By Jacobi's theory H is then the conjugate point (it lies on the envelope), so the arc is at best a degenerate, non-strict extremal, not a proper minimum.

On the next page Euler claims that both parabolic arcs can be minima when gg < fh. This is false for the high lob: it touches the envelope (passes a conjugate point) before reaching H, so it is not even a weak local minimum. Only the low arc is a local minimum.

Euler never determines when the smooth arc stops being the global minimum compared with the broken path. Hence 'paradox' is only partly resolved: for g below a threshold the low parabola is the global minimum, above it the broken path is.

ideas.what: Real extremals exist iff g² ≤ fh: the reachable region is bounded by the envelope (safety parabola), and two arcs coalesce on it.
ideas.modern_name: envelope of extremals / caustic; safety parabola; boundary of the conjugate locus
ideas.usually_credited_to: Safety parabola: Torricelli. Conjugate-point theory: Jacobi (1836).
ideas.where_published: E735 itself (Mém. Acad. St-Pétersbourg III, 1811). Possibly related remarks in Euler's ballistics/projectile writings — unsure.

ideas.what: A broken path along the zero-velocity line has smaller action than the smooth extremal and is a minimum 'in its kind'.
ideas.modern_name: Goldschmidt-type discontinuous solution; degenerate Jacobi–Maupertuis metric at the Hill (zero-velocity) boundary
ideas.usually_credited_to: Goldschmidt (1831) for the minimal surface of revolution; Weierstrass/Erdmann for broken extremals; modern Jacobi-metric degeneracy discussed by e.g. Seifert and Montgomery.

ideas.what: The broken path satisfies the first integral p√x/√(1+p²) = C piecewise with C = 0, so it is 'contained in the calculus'.
ideas.modern_name: piecewise satisfaction of the Euler–Lagrange first integral (Beltrami/Noether-type invariant); Erdmann corner condition at the singular boundary x = 0
superadditivity of a convex power function

missed.claim: Euler never computes the threshold at which the low parabola stops being the global minimum and the broken path takes over. For f = h the low-arc action is (2/3)f^{3/2}(2+t)√(2−2t), with t = √(f²−g²)/f. Setting it equal to (4/3)f^{3/2} gives t² + 2t − 2 = 0, so t = √3 − 1. The threshold is g = f√(2√3 − 3) ≈ 0.681 f, against the reachability limit g = f. Between these values the low parabola is only a local minimum. This is the exact analogue of the Goldschmidt threshold for the catenoid.
missed.quote: quod manifesto semper minus est quam illud, quod pro arcu parabolico FH invenimus, etiamsi hoc in suo genere sit minimum
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It gives a clean, exactly solvable Goldschmidt-type exchange-of-minimum example in the Jacobi–Maupertuis setting, from about 20 years before Goldschmidt. Useful historically and pedagogically.

missed.claim: Euler notes that the action vanishes along the zero-velocity line and that paths running along it satisfy the extremal condition. This anticipates the modern observation that the Jacobi–Maupertuis metric degenerates on the Hill boundary, where boundary segments have zero length and 'brake orbits'/broken geodesics appear.
missed.quote: at vero pro via horizontali fh, propter x = 0, iterum evanescit
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is an early explicit instance of the degenerate-boundary phenomenon in variational mechanics. To my knowledge it is not cited in the modern Jacobi-metric literature (unsure).

missed.claim: The coalescence of the two arcs at gg = fh, with the longest throw on the envelope, is precisely the conjugate-point situation. Euler notices the paradox but misreads it as two coexisting minima rather than a failure of minimality past the envelope. This is a missed link to the Jacobi condition 25 years early.
missed.quote: siquidem tum binae solutiones in unam coalescunt, ob √(fh−gg)=0; tum vero arcus parabolicus FH jactum longissimum repraesentabit
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical precursor of the role of envelopes in Jacobi's theory (Jacobi 1836) that is worth crediting.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a genuine posthumous Euler discussion of a Goldschmidt-type broken minimizer and an envelope/conjugate-point paradox for the Maupertuis action, well before Goldschmidt and Jacobi. The paper is catalogued and probably mentioned in some histories, so it is not entirely unknown. The exchange threshold and the correct conjugate-point reading are absent from the page.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image; ∂.(p√x/√(1+pp)) = 0 is correctly read, as is the exponent 3/2 in (2/3)(f+h)^{3/2}.
